page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: An isolated system is a system that can
exchange neither matter nor energy with
steps.why: The three system types differ only in what crosses the boundary: an open system passes both matter and energy, a closed system passes only energy, and an isolated system passes neither.
common_mistakes: Confusing isolated with closed — a closed system still exchanges energy.
Saying only that it is closed on all sides. The answer must name both matter and energy.
steps.memory_tip: Isolated blocks both: no matter, no energy. Closed blocks only matter.
steps.margin_note: Both words — matter and energy — must appear.

steps.label: The example
lines: Example: hot water sealed in a thermos
flask. No water leaves, and the insulated
walls let almost no heat pass.

lines.text: Isolated: no matter and no energy cross the boundary

steps.why: A thermos flask is the standard example, although it is only approximately isolated — over many hours some heat still passes its walls. The source book prints the example as ice in a thermos flask; the hot water written above is the same physics in the same container, and either wording earns the mark.
common_mistakes: Giving an open beaker or a sealed metal can as the example — the first is open, the second is closed.
steps.memory_tip: One picture: a sealed, insulated flask. Sealed stops matter; insulation stops energy.
steps.margin_note: The book prints ice in a thermos flask; the hot water written here is the same idea. Any sealed insulated flask is accepted.

insider_note: The definition mark needs both halves — no matter AND no energy — and the example mark needs a container that blocks both, which is why the thermos flask is the expected answer.
